meta.title: way1ong Sky — a flight through the Solar System
meta.description: Fly between the Sun, the planets and the Moon — where they really are today. Free, no ads, no tracking.

app.name: Sky
app.scene: The Solar System in 3D. Drag to look around, pinch or scroll to come closer; pick a body from the list to fly to it.

scale.label: Scale
scale.handyNote: Handy scale: distances squeezed, bodies enlarged — everything fits one look. Directions are real.
scale.trueNote: True scale: sizes and distances as they are. The planets are specks in an emptiness — fly to one to see it.

time.label: Time
time.noSpin: At this speed the bodies’ spin about their own axes is not shown: it would only flicker. Their motion along the orbits is real.
time.limit: The app’s calendar ends here: it runs from {from} to {to}.

lunarAt.total: {date}: a total lunar eclipse. The whole Moon is in the Earth’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the shadow leave.
lunarAt.partial: {date}: a partial lunar eclipse. Part of the Moon is in the Earth’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the shadow move.

solarAt.total: {date}: a total solar eclipse. The dark spot on the Earth is the Moon’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the spot cross the Earth.
solarAt.annular: {date}: an annular solar eclipse. The dim spot on the Earth is the Moon’s shadow; a ring of the Sun stays visible there. Time is stopped — let it run to watch the spot cross the Earth.
solarAt.partial: {date}: a partial solar eclipse. The dim patch on the Earth is the edge of the Moon’s shadow. Time is stopped — let it run to watch it move.

about.sun: The Sun is the star at the heart of our solar system, and the only star in it. It is a huge ball of hydrogen and helium held together by its own gravity, and it holds 99.8% of the solar system’s mass. Its gravity keeps everything in orbit, from the biggest planets to the smallest bits of debris.
about.mercury: Mercury is the planet closest to the Sun and the smallest one, only slightly larger than the Earth’s Moon. Days there reach 430 °C; with no atmosphere to keep the heat, nights drop to −180 °C. It is the fastest planet: it goes around the Sun in 88 Earth days.
about.venus: Venus is the second planet from the Sun and the Earth’s closest planetary neighbor; in our sky it is the third brightest object after the Sun and the Moon. It is similar to the Earth in structure and size, but its thick atmosphere traps heat and makes it the hottest planet, with a surface hot enough to melt lead. Venus spins slowly, and in the opposite direction from most planets.
about.earth: The Earth is the third planet from the Sun and the biggest of the four planets closest to it, all made of rock and metal. It is the only place we know of inhabited by living things, and the only planet in the solar system with liquid water on its surface. Its atmosphere is 78% nitrogen, 21% oxygen and 1% other gases, and it shields us from much of the Sun’s harmful radiation.
about.moon: The Moon is the Earth’s only natural satellite. It spins at the same rate as it goes around the Earth, so the same side always faces us; people first saw the far side in 1959, when a Soviet spacecraft flew past. Its surface is solid and rocky, cratered and pitted by impacts of asteroids, meteorites and comets.
about.mars: Mars is the fourth planet from the Sun. It is called the Red Planet: iron minerals in its dirt oxidize, or rust, and make the surface look red. It is one of the most explored bodies in the solar system and the only planet where rovers have been sent; NASA missions have found lots of evidence that billions of years ago Mars was much wetter and warmer, with a thicker atmosphere.
about.jupiter: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun and the largest in the solar system — more than twice as massive as all the other planets combined. Its stripes and swirls are cold, windy clouds of ammonia and water in an atmosphere of hydrogen and helium. The Great Red Spot is a giant storm bigger than the Earth that has raged for hundreds of years.
about.saturn: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun and the second largest. Like Jupiter, it is a massive ball made mostly of hydrogen and helium. It is not the only planet with rings, but none are as spectacular or as complex as Saturn’s. It is the farthest planet from the Earth discovered by the unaided eye, known since ancient times.
about.uranus: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun and the third largest — a very cold and windy world. It rotates at a nearly 90-degree angle from the plane of its orbit, so it appears to spin sideways, rolling around the Sun like a ball. It was the first planet found with the aid of a telescope: the astronomer William Herschel discovered it in 1781.
about.neptune: Neptune is the eighth and most distant planet from the Sun, more than 30 times as far from it as the Earth. It is a dark, cold ice giant whipped by supersonic winds, and the only planet in our solar system not visible to the naked eye. It was discovered in 1846 and completed its first orbit around the Sun since then in 2011.

photo.sun: The Sun on 10 September 2025, taken by NASA’s Solar Dynamics Observatory in extreme ultraviolet light. Our eyes cannot see this light; the gold colour is added.

photo.earth: The Earth, photographed by the Apollo 17 crew on 7 December 1972 on their way to the Moon. Almost the whole coastline of Africa is in view, with the Arabian Peninsula above and the south polar ice cap of Antarctica below.
photo.moon: The Moon, photographed on 6 April 2026 during NASA’s Artemis II mission. The near side, with its dark ancient lava flows, is the top half; the large crater below them is the Orientale basin, and everything below it is the far side.
photo.mars: Mars: a global colour view from Viking images.
photo.jupiter: Jupiter in true colour: four images taken by NASA’s Cassini spacecraft on 7 December 2000, projected onto a globe. The dark spot is the shadow of Jupiter’s moon Europa.
photo.saturn: Saturn and its rings in natural colour, taken by the Cassini spacecraft on 27 March 2004, on approach to the planet.
photo.uranus: Uranus, taken by the Voyager 2 spacecraft in 1986.
photo.neptune: Neptune, from the last whole-planet images of NASA’s Voyager 2, taken 4 days and 20 hours before its closest approach. The Great Dark Spot is in view.

text.sun: In Latin the Sun is “sol”, and the Sun god of the ancient Greeks was Helios: words like “solar” and “heliosphere” come from them. Several spacecraft watch the Sun; the SOHO observatory has done so since its launch in 1995. In 2021 NASA’s Parker Solar Probe became the first spacecraft to fly through the corona, the Sun’s upper atmosphere.
text.mercury: Mercury is named for the swiftest of the ancient Roman gods; it is one of the five bright planets the Romans could see in the sky. The first spacecraft to visit it was NASA’s Mariner 10, launched in 1973; the first to orbit it was MESSENGER, launched in 2004. In 2018 Europe and Japan launched BepiColombo, a joint mission of two spacecraft.
text.venus: Venus is named for the ancient Roman goddess of love and beauty — the only planet named after a female god. The ancients took it for two objects, a morning star and an evening star. Its phases, first observed by Galileo through his telescope, gave the key proof that the planets go round the Sun. On December 14, 1962, NASA’s Mariner 2 flew past Venus — the first visit of a spacecraft to another planet. Between 1961 and 1984 ten Soviet Venera probes reached its surface.
text.earth: Earth is the only planet whose English name does not come from Greek or Roman mythology: the word is about 1,000 years old and simply means “the ground”. Every language has its own name for our planet. Today many spacecraft in orbit study the Earth as a whole system — the atmosphere, the ocean, the glaciers and the solid ground.
text.moon: The Moon shares its name with all moons because people did not know of others until Galileo discovered four moons of Jupiter in 1610. In 1959 the Soviet Luna 1 was the first spacecraft to fly by the Moon, in 1966 Luna 9 made the first soft landing, and in 1969 Apollo 11 landed the first people. From 1969 to 1972 twelve American astronauts walked on the Moon. In April 2026 Artemis II carried four astronauts around its far side.
text.mars: The ancient Romans named Mars for their god of war because its reddish color reminded them of blood; the Egyptians called it “Her Desher”, the red one. In the list of missions to Mars that NASA keeps, the first flyby that did not fail is Mariner 4, launched in 1964; the first orbiters were launched in 1971, and the first lander with a rover, Mars Pathfinder, in 1996. Mars is the only planet where rovers roam.
text.jupiter: Jupiter shines bright, so people have known it since ancient times; it is named for the king of the Roman gods. In 1610 Galileo Galilei made the first detailed observations of it with a small homemade telescope and saw its four largest moons. NASA’s first spacecraft to the outer planets, Pioneer 10, came closest to Jupiter on December 4, 1973. The Galileo spacecraft orbited the planet for almost eight years, and on July 4, 2016, Juno entered orbit around it.
text.saturn: Saturn is the farthest planet found by the unaided eye, known since ancient times; the oldest written records of it, about 700 BCE, are attributed to the Assyrians. It is named for the Roman god of agriculture. In 1610 Galileo saw its rings but took them for a “triple planet”; in 1655 Christiaan Huygens discovered the rings and the largest moon, Titan. Pioneer 11 was the first spacecraft to reach Saturn, on September 1, 1979; on July 1, 2004, Cassini became the first to orbit it, and on January 14, 2005, the Huygens probe landed on Titan.
text.uranus: Uranus was the first planet found with a telescope: the British astronomer William Herschel discovered it on March 13, 1781, taking it at first for a comet or a star. He wanted to name it after King George III, but the name suggested by Johann Bode — that of the Greek god of the sky — was the one that stayed. Only one spacecraft has visited it: on January 24, 1986, Voyager 2 passed 81,500 kilometers from its cloud tops and discovered 10 new moons and two new rings.
text.neptune: Neptune was the first planet found by calculation: Uranus did not move as expected, and the French mathematician Urbain Le Verrier worked out where an unknown planet should be. In 1846 Johann Galle at the Berlin Observatory found it on his first night of searching. Galileo had seen Neptune in 1612 and 1613 but recorded it as a fixed star. The planet is named for the Roman god of the sea. Only one spacecraft has studied it up close: Voyager 2, in 1989.

about.io: Io is the most volcanically active world in the solar system, with hundreds of volcanoes; some throw lava fountains dozens of kilometers high. It is caught between Jupiter’s massive gravity and the precisely timed pulls of its neighbors Europa and Ganymede. The volcanoes cover its face with new deposits faster than large craters can mark it. Voyager 1 spotted the first signs of this volcanism in 1979; most of what we know about Io comes from the Galileo spacecraft.
about.europa: There is strong evidence that the icy moon Europa has a saltwater ocean — perhaps one of the best places to look for environments where life could exist beyond Earth. Europa is the fourth largest of Jupiter’s moons. Most of what we know about it comes from the Galileo mission; on October 14, 2024, NASA launched Europa Clipper, the first mission to study Europa in detail.
about.ganymede: Ganymede is the largest moon in the solar system, bigger even than the planet Mercury. It is the only moon known to have its own magnetic field, which causes auroras around its poles. The dark areas of its surface are older and heavily cratered, the light ones younger. There is strong evidence of an underground saltwater ocean that may hold more water than all of Earth’s surface. The Juno spacecraft photographed it in detail in June 2021.
about.callisto: Callisto is the most heavily cratered object in the solar system. It is Jupiter’s second largest moon and the third largest in the solar system. Data from the Galileo spacecraft in the 1990s showed that it may hide a salty ocean beneath its surface. Callisto and Jupiter’s three other largest moons were discovered in 1610 by the Italian scientist Galileo Galilei.

keys: Arrow keys turn the view, plus and minus change the distance.

about.title: About
about.text: The bodies stand where they really are today; the positions are computed on your device. Nothing is sent anywhere: no ads, no tracking, no account.
about.textures: Maps of the Sun, the planets and the Moon, and the starry background: Solar System Scope, CC BY 4.0. The background is decoration: its stars are not placed by a catalogue.
about.moonMaps: Maps of Jupiter’s four moons: Credit: U.S. Geological Survey, from images of the Voyager and Galileo spacecraft; public domain. The maps are in shades of grey and have no images near the poles. The moons turn one side to Jupiter — which side is shown only roughly; the moons’ shadows and eclipses are not drawn.
about.facts: Sizes of the bodies and of Saturn’s rings: NASA fact sheets.
about.shadows: The Earth’s shadow on the Moon and the Moon’s on the Earth are computed from the real positions. The copper glow of the eclipsed Moon is a picture, not a measurement.
about.aim: “Point the phone” on the sky map is a trial. The program reads the phone’s tilt and compass on the device only and sends them nowhere. A phone’s compass is rough, so the sky on the screen may be shifted against the real one; the picture does not lean with the phone.
about.photos: Photos in the cards: NASA and its partners, named under each photo; some are cropped. This program is made independently of NASA.
about.sky: The sky from a place: stars — Wikidata (CC0); which stars are joined into constellations — d3-celestial by Olaf Frohn (BSD-3-Clause), after the charts of the IAU and Sky & Telescope; cities — Wikidata. Stars are drawn by day too, and the bending of light by the air near the horizon is not drawn. “Dark enough”, “in view” and “too faint for the eye” are the program’s own measures, not definitions of astronomy. For some stars Wikidata has no visual brightness: there the close Gaia G brightness is used. Proper names of stars: the names approved by the International Astronomical Union, from the list in Wikipedia (CC BY-SA 4.0), and the titles of the stars’ articles in Wikipedia.
about.stories: The stories of the constellations are written after Wikipedia’s articles — the links to the articles stand under each story. The texts of the stories may be used under the same licence, CC BY-SA 4.0. The brightest star, the month of the best evenings and the height of a constellation are worked out by the program itself.

listed.ptolemy: One of the 48 constellations listed by the astronomer Ptolemy in the 2nd century. Since 1922 it has been on the International Astronomical Union’s list of 88 constellations.

about.Ori: Orion is a hunter of Greek mythology — a giant, a son of Poseidon, the god of the sea. Its seven brightest stars draw an hourglass: four of them make a large rectangle, and in its middle lie the three stars of Orion’s Belt. In one myth Orion boasted that he would kill every animal on Earth, and the angry goddess Gaia sent a scorpion against him (in other tellings it was Artemis or Apollo) — which is given as the reason why Orion and Scorpius are never in the sky at the same time.
about.Tau: Taurus, the Bull, is a constellation of the zodiac, and people have seen a bull in it since very old times. In Greek mythology it is Zeus, who took the form of a magnificent white bull to carry off Europa, a Phoenician princess. Old pictures show only the front half of the bull — explained by his being half under water as he carried Europa out to sea. In another myth it is Io, a lover of Zeus, whom he turned into a heifer to hide her from his wife Hera.
about.Aur: The Latin name Auriga means “the charioteer”. The constellation is drawn as a chariot driver who holds a goat over his left shoulder and two kids under his arm. In Greek mythology he is most often Erichthonius, a king of Athens raised by the goddess Athena: he is credited with inventing the four-horse chariot, and Zeus placed him in the heavens. In another version he is the charioteer Myrtilus, set in the sky after his death by his father Hermes. The brightest star, Capella, is tied to the she-goat Amalthea, who nursed the infant Zeus.
about.Gem: The name is Latin for “twins”: they are Castor and Pollux of Greek mythology, the sons of Leda, both of them Argonauts. In the usual telling they had different fathers: Castor was the mortal son of Tyndareus, king of Sparta, and Pollux the son of Zeus. When Castor died, Pollux begged Zeus to give his brother immortality, and Zeus united them in the heavens. Two bright stars of the constellation bear their names.
about.Per: The constellation is named after Perseus, a hero of Greek mythology and the son of Danaë. King Polydectes sent him to bring the head of Medusa the Gorgon, whose face turned to stone all who looked at her; Perseus slew her in her sleep. Going on, he rescued Andromeda, the daughter of King Cepheus, who was to be sacrificed to a sea monster — in one version he killed it with his sword, in another he turned it to stone with Medusa’s head. In the sky Perseus lies near Andromeda, Cepheus, Cassiopeia, Cetus and Pegasus.
about.Cas: The constellation is named after Cassiopeia of Greek mythology — the queen of Aethiopia, wife of King Cepheus and mother of Andromeda. It is easy to recognise by its “W” of five bright stars. Cassiopeia boasted that her daughter was more beautiful than the Nereids, the sea nymphs (or, in another telling, that she herself was), and the enraged Poseidon sent a sea monster against her country. As a punishment she was placed in the sky on her throne and made to wheel around the north celestial pole, clinging to it half of the time so as not to fall off.
about.And: The constellation is named for Andromeda of the Greek myth, the daughter of Cassiopeia and King Cepheus; in English it is also known as “the Chained Lady”. When Cassiopeia bragged that her daughter was more beautiful than the sea nymphs, Poseidon sent the sea monster Cetus against Aethiopia, and an oracle said that only the sacrifice of the princess would save the kingdom. Andromeda was chained to a rock by the sea, but the hero Perseus saved her — in one version he turned the monster to stone with the head of Medusa, in another he slew it with his sword. They married, and after her death Athena placed Andromeda in the sky. The neighbouring constellations Perseus, Cassiopeia and Cepheus are other characters of the same myth.
about.Peg: The constellation is named after Pegasus, the winged horse of Greek mythology. He was born from the blood of Medusa when Perseus cut off her head. One myth says that his hooves dug out the spring Hippocrene, whose water gave the gift of poetry. Pegasus became the horse of Bellerophon, who killed the Chimera with his help; but when Bellerophon asked to be carried to Mount Olympus, Zeus made the horse throw him off. Three stars of Pegasus and one of Andromeda form the large Square of Pegasus.
about.UMa: Its Latin name means “greater bear”, and many peoples have seen a bear in these stars. Its seven main stars are the Big Dipper, also called the Plough or the Wagon. In the Greek myth the nymph Callisto bore Zeus a son, Arcas, and Zeus’s jealous wife Hera turned her into a bear. When Arcas later met the bear and almost speared her, Zeus whisked them both into the sky: Callisto as Ursa Major and Arcas as Boötes (in another telling, as the Little Bear).
about.UMi: Ursa Minor is Latin for “Lesser Bear”; its seven stars make a smaller ladle, the Little Dipper, with four stars in the bowl. It holds Polaris, the north pole star, and so has long been important to mariners. There is no single myth of it. In one tradition it is a nymph, a nurse of Zeus, whom the god honoured with a place in the sky; in another, two bears saved the infant Zeus from his father Cronus by hiding him on Mount Ida, and he later set them in the sky — their tails growing long as he swung them up.
